questions.question: What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ when $\boldsymbol{x} \neq \boldsymbol{y}$?
options: $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|$
$\infty$

questions.question: What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})$?
options: $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|$

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge1$, what is the relationship between the discrete metric and the usual $p$-metrics, $1\le p\le\infty$, in terms of strong equivalence?
options: The discrete metric is equal to every $p$-metric
The discrete metric is strongly equivalent to exactly one of the $p$-metrics
The discrete metric is not a metric
The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the $p$-metrics

questions.question: What determines the value of the discrete metric?
options: The Euclidean distance between the two points.
Whether the two points are equal or distinct.
The angle between the two points.
The dimension of the ambient space only.

questions.question: What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}((1,2),(3,4))$?
options: $\sqrt{8}$

questions.question: If $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \lt 1$, what must be true?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{y}$.
$d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=1$.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ must be real numbers rather than vectors.
$\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the discrete metric $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$, let $x_n=\tfrac{1}{n}$ for $n=1,2,\dots$. Does $(x_n)$ converge to $0$?
options: Yes, because $\tfrac{1}{n}\to0$ in the usual sense of $|x-y|$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
Yes, because $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x_n,0)\le1$ for every $n$, so the terms stay near $0$.
No, because $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x_n,0)=1$ for every $n$, so the distances never become small.
No, because $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x_n,0)$ grows without bound as $n$ increases.

questions.question: Why is there no constant $b>0$ with $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,y)\le b\,|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$?
options: Distinct points can be arbitrarily close in $|x-y|$ while $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,y)=1$, so $1\le b\,|x-y|$ fails for them.
$|x-y|$ can be arbitrarily large for distinct points while $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,y)$ never exceeds $1$.
Such a $b$ does exist: $b=1$ works, because $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,y)\le1$ holds for all $x,y$.
The metric $|x-y|$ comes from a norm and $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ does not, so no inequality between them can hold.

questions.question: Fix $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and for $r>0$ let $S_r=\{\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})<r\}$. How does $S_r$ depend on $r$?
options: $S_r=\{\boldsymbol{x}\}$ for $0<r\le1$ and $S_r=\mathbb{R}^n$ for $r>1$.
$S_r=\{\boldsymbol{x}\}$ for $0<r<1$ and $S_r=\mathbb{R}^n$ for $r\ge1$.
$S_r$ gains points one at a time as $r$ grows, like the Euclidean set $\{\boldsymbol{y}\colon\|\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}\|<r\}$.
$S_r=\mathbb{R}^n$ for every $r>0$, because all points are within distance $1$ of $\boldsymbol{x}$.

questions.question: Let $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ be the discrete metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$: $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=1$ if $\boldsymbol{x}\ne \boldsymbol{y}$ and $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0$ if $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}$. Which argument correctly proves $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z})\le d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})+d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z})$ for all $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: If $\boldsymbol{x}\ne \boldsymbol{z}$, then $\boldsymbol{y}$ differs from both $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{z}$, so the right side equals $2$ and exceeds the left side; if $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{z}$ the left side is $0$.
The right side is a sum of two distances and so is always at least $1$, while the left side is never larger than $1$.

If $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{z}$ the left side is $0$; if $\boldsymbol{x}\ne \boldsymbol{z}$, then $\boldsymbol{y}$ differs from at least one of $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{z}$, so the right side is at least $1$.

Since $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0$ exactly when $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|=0$, the metric $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ inherits the triangle inequality of the Euclidean distance.
